NC-2025-HB1035.s: The law changes election rules for the City of Marion and the Town of Old Fort. It moves their municipal elections to even-numbered years, changes some council and alderman terms, and skips elections there in 2027. Marion and Old Fort will resume regular elections in 2028 under the new schedule.

NC-2025-HB1040.s: The bill updates the Pitt County-City of Greenville Airport Authority’s rules on money, land, and airport projects. It changes how Pitt County and the City of Greenville can budget for airport costs, approve extra land, and use bonds or other funds for airport work. It also updates old legal cross-references and says the authority board members are not public officers for certain state law rules. The act takes effect when it becomes law.

NC-2025-HB1067.s: The bill would set a noon July 6, 2026 deadline for candidates using petitions to seek municipal office in the 2026 election, filed with the county board of elections. The main changes would take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, and would apply to elections in 2028 and later.

NC-2025-HB1083.s: The bill would create a voluntary portable benefits account system for independent contractors. Hiring parties could put money into these accounts, but the worker would have to agree in writing and could opt out at any time. The money could be used for things like health coverage, retirement savings, disability insurance, and life insurance, and the bill sets tax rules and reporting rules for these accounts. It would take effect January 1, 2027, and apply to tax years starting on or after that date.

NC-2025-HB1094.s: This act became law and makes several changes for the City of Durham. It lets Durham set a lower default speed limit of at least 20 miles per hour on city streets that are not part of the state highway system, with gateway signs and a public map. It also sets faster review steps for Durham requests to change speed limits on state highways. The act includes a technical fix for motor vehicle dealer rules, with that part set to take effect on October 1, 2026.

NC-2025-HB1104.s: North Carolina's law would change parts of the involuntary commitment process and rules tied to public safety. It would also affect courts, sheriffs, the Department of Health and Human Services, and some mental health and restoration programs by changing how records, treatment plans, and shared information can be used. The law was ratified and signed by the governor on July 6, 2026.

NC-2025-HB1126.s: North Carolina enacted a bill with technical and clarifying changes to the State Treasurer laws and to the rules for a legislative oversight commission. It gives that commission broader access to records, data, buildings, and some payroll systems from state, local, and some public-funded entities, and it keeps certain information confidential. It also makes it a Class 2 misdemeanor to hide, destroy, change, or refuse to provide required material to the commission.

NC-2025-HB116.s: The law adds certain parts of Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune, Marine Corps Air Station New River, and Marine Corps Special Operations Command at Stones Bay and the New River to the City of Jacksonville. It says these areas will be subject to city taxes for tax years starting on or after July 1, 2026, and it limits the city’s power to regulate federal activities at those bases. It also changes where Jacksonville police can use arrest powers and says the city may not annex land south of N.C. Highway 24 or use city land-use powers outside its contiguous city limits.

NC-2025-HB117.s: North Carolina enacted a law about parking fees in Ocean Isle Beach and Topsail Beach. The change lets those towns handle parking fees, and the short title was updated to match. It was ratified on June 25, 2026.

NC-2025-HB1173.s: The law makes it a crime for a member of a criminal gang to use, carry, or have a firearm during or in support of a serious felony, drug crime, or violent crime. The penalty would be a Class G felony, with higher charges if the gun is shown or fired. It defines terms like firearm, serious felony, drug crime, and violent crime for this offense.

NC-2025-HB1200.s: Would make certain family essentials tax-free, likely including items tied to health, pregnancy, newborns, and hygiene. An adopted amendment changes one date in the bill from October 1, 2026, to April 1, 2027.

NC-2025-HB1213.s: The bill would change the property tax break for solar energy electric systems. Systems placed in service on or after July 1, 2027, would no longer get the 80% property tax exclusion. The change would apply to taxes for taxable years beginning on or after July 1, 2027.

NC-2025-HB1220.s: This law makes a set of local changes for several North Carolina counties and towns. The listed topics include alcohol rules, annexation, city and county government, planning and zoning, law enforcement, and wildlife and coastal matters. It was ratified on July 2, 2026.

NC-2025-HB1222.s: The act would give the Brunswick County Board of Commissioners the final say on certain land use decisions, including some subdivision plats, special use permits, zoning changes, and variances. It would also require traffic impact studies for certain development projects and have those studies presented in open meetings before a vote. The board’s final votes on these matters would have to be recorded so the public record shows how each member voted, and the rule would apply only in Brunswick County outside city zoning areas.

NC-2025-HB1240.s: The bill would ask voters to approve a change to the North Carolina Constitution that would give people the right to early voting in primary and general elections held in even-numbered years. It would require at least 14 days of early voting, set minimum hours for early voting sites, and let county election boards set sites and staffing. It would also allow same-day voter registration during early voting.

NC-2025-HB1242.s: The bill would change the North Carolina Constitution to update the wording of the "law of the land" clause. It would send that change to voters at the statewide general election on November 3, 2026. If most voters approve it, the amendment would take effect when the vote is certified.

NC-2025-HB1246.s: The bill would add rules against using troops or armed people at voting places near Election Day, with some exceptions for law enforcement and emergency help. It would also make voter threats, coercion, and certain false voter challenges crimes, create money for voter education, and let people seek court orders and damages if they are targeted. The bill would also protect election workers from threats, change early voting hours for all county sites, and start those early voting changes on January 1, 2027. The visible text also begins a new section on election certification, but no new rule is shown yet.

NC-2025-HB133.s: This law changes how a deed or other land record is filed when it covers certain land tied to farmland and military protection rules. The person filing the deed must attach the needed affidavit, and the register of deeds is not responsible for checking or enforcing that step. If the affidavit is missing, it does not change notice, lien order, validity, or insurance of the record.

NC-2025-HB147.s: This law makes several local changes in North Carolina. It includes changes for Currituck County and changes to how primary elections are run in the city of Hickory.

NC-2025-HB169.s: The bill would change occupancy taxes for Haywood County and the Town of Leland, and it would change the tourism group rules in Haywood and Cherokee counties. In Haywood County, it would raise and add room occupancy taxes, set how the money is split and spent for travel and tourism, and change who serves on the tourism development authority. In Cherokee County, it would update the tourism development authority’s membership rules and terms.

NC-2025-HB171.s: The bill bans state agencies and local governments from using public money for diversity, equity, and inclusion programs or training, and from keeping DEI offices or staff. It also bars these bodies from using DEI in hiring, jobs, or contracts, and sets civil penalties and court actions for violations. The new state-agency rules take effect July 1, 2026, and apply to acts on or after that date.

NC-2025-HB198.s: The bill would change how profits from the Town of Angier ABC Board are split. It would send 10% to recreation programs in Angier, let 10% be used for alcohol education and rehab work, and send the rest to the town’s general fund, with up to 25% of that share able to go to recreation. Any old funds held for the Angier Community Library would instead go to recreation programs in town.

NC-2025-HB199.s: The bill would create a process for towns and cities to remove land from their borders, and for property owners to ask for that change too. It would require public notice, a public hearing, and a report on how the change would affect city money and services; in some cases, local voters in the area could also vote on it. The bill also sets rules for petitions, hearing notices, and what happens to city services after land is removed.

NC-2025-HB206.s: The law makes several changes to public safety and victim help programs in North Carolina. It lets the Department of Public Safety and the Air National Guard sign a new 50-year land use license for part of the Stanly County Airport, and it allows state disaster-response trailers and utility vehicles to be given to local governments, nonprofits, or survivors needing long-term housing help. It raises some crime victim compensation limits, changes claim rules and privacy sharing, and lets tribal police chiefs enter mutual aid agreements with other law enforcement agencies. It also changes how the Adjutant General is appointed and confirmed by the Governor and the General Assembly.

NC-2025-HB268.s: North Carolina Session Law 2026-61 makes technical and clarifying changes to the 2026 state budget and other laws. It shifts $500,000 from the State Auditor to the State Board of Elections, changes how directed grants are paid out, and makes several changes to state rules on budget adjustments, local board appointments, and town planning powers. It also includes disaster relief funding changes tied to Hurricane Helene.

NC-2025-HB301.s: The bill would change rules for addictive social media platforms in North Carolina. It would set limits tied to foreign ownership, allow accounts for 14- and 15-year-olds to be closed if there is no parent or guardian consent after a 30-day chance to dispute, and say certain internet and tech providers are not covered just for helping deliver a platform they do not control. The section in the amendment would take effect January 1, 2027, and apply to cases that arise on or after that date.

NC-2025-HB308.s: The bill would make a range of criminal law changes in North Carolina. It includes rules on ignition interlock credit for people with out-of-state convictions, rights to information about sexual assault evidence kits, and changes to some crime penalties. It would also affect people and groups tied to metals recycling, pardons of innocence, and access to felony conviction records.

NC-2025-HB328.s: The bill would set rules for selling, shipping, and having hemp-derived consumable products in North Carolina. It would require licenses, age checks for buyers under 30 in some cases, child-resistant packaging, and testing and labeling rules, and it would bar sales of some products with more than 0.3% delta-9 THC or certain other hemp cannabinoids. It would also add kratom as a Schedule VI controlled substance and set civil fines and possible criminal penalties for some violations.

NC-2025-HB34.s: This bill would tighten rules for Medicaid providers in North Carolina. It would change the grounds for adverse termination, including false claims for services not provided, falsifying medical records, and not repaying a final overpayment of more than $1,500. It would also allow action for conduct that may put Medicaid patients or the program at risk, and it would add the words "lawfully present" in one place.

NC-2025-HB349.s: The bill would update North Carolina rules for health care powers of attorney and advance health care directives, which let a person name someone to make health care choices if they cannot do so. It would also let the Secretary of State receive advance health care directives filed online. The bill would change the rules for qualified witnesses and update the standard form and instructions for these documents.

NC-2025-HB356.s: Would make several changes to civil and insurance laws in North Carolina.

NC-2025-HB372.s: Cities in North Carolina would not be allowed to ban certain low-impact home-based businesses or require permits, licenses, or similar approvals for them. These businesses must be run from a home, stay mostly inside or in the yard, not cause much traffic or street parking, and follow state and federal law. The law also says cities cannot require rezoning to commercial use or fire sprinklers just for these businesses, but homeowners association rules and deed limits still apply.

NC-2025-HB376.s: Creates changes tied to water and wastewater affordability and system capacity in North Carolina, and it became law.

NC-2025-HB377.s: The bill would make a range of court changes, including in civil cases, court fees, records, and other court rules. It would clarify the difference between court costs and court expenses, and it would set fee amounts for use of court facilities in certain civil actions. It would also add a $20 fee for filing a notice of hearing on certain motions, with some exceptions, and it would take effect when it becomes law and apply to cases already pending or filed after that date.

NC-2025-HB437.s: The bill would change rules tied to drug-free zones and public camping. It would also define certain shelters for homeless people as a kind of service facility and set a notice-and-fix process for claims against a local government, including 15 business days to correct the issue. It would affect homeless service providers and local governments.

NC-2025-HB481.s: The law changes the special separation allowance for state and local law enforcement officers. It sets new rules for who can get the payment, how the amount is figured, and when the payments stop. It also changes when some retired officers can return to state work without losing the allowance. It took effect when it became law.

NC-2025-HB517.s: The law changes parts of North Carolina’s rules for nonprofit corporations and charitable groups. It also extends some emergency video notary rules until July 1, 2027, or until the first license is issued under a new licensing law, whichever happens first. Notarial acts made under those rules stay valid and do not need to be done again.

NC-2025-HB56.s: This act makes technical and clarifying changes to the 2026 state budget and other laws. It changes some funding for disaster relief, the Town of Fair Bluff riverwalk project, school funding, and the State Textbook Fund, and it sets new principal pay schedules and salary supplements for 2026-2027. It also sets out how some education savings would be used for school nutrition staff, literacy training, and math curriculum work.

NC-2025-HB562.s: The law makes budget and technical changes to North Carolina spending for 2026-2027. It shifts some grant funds, including $1.5 million for hyperbaric oxygen therapy for veterans and changes grants for Harnett County and Anson County. It also updates rules for some license plates and adds recurring General Fund money for the State Fire Marshal and the Department of Labor. Most parts take effect July 1, 2026, and the law was signed on August 11, 2026.

NC-2025-HB565.s: The bill would limit the use of artificial intelligence in health insurance reviews and in health care billing. It would bar an AI-based tool from being the only reason to deny a review or prior authorization decision, and it would stop health care providers and AI developers from using AI for coding, billing, or records work if the system is made to push upcoding, which means billing for a higher level of care than was given. Beginning July 1, 2027, health care providers would also have to file yearly proof that they follow these rules to stay in Medicaid.

NC-2025-HB600.s: The bill would give official state recognition to The Tuscarora Indians of Kahtenuaka Territories starting July 1, 2026. It would also add two Tuscarora members to the State Commission of Indian Affairs and one Tuscarora representative to the American Indian Heritage Commission. The bill sets aside $5,000 for the Department of Administration and $5,000 for Natural and Cultural Resources to update websites and other materials.

NC-2025-HB747.s: North Carolina’s wildlife law changes became law. The act tightens privacy rules for some Wildlife Resources Commission records, creates new special license plates, and changes some boating safety and registration rules. It also lets the Wildlife Resources Commission sell one elk permit by raffle and one by auction for the 2027 hunting season, with the money going to elk conservation and management.

NC-2025-HB83.s: North Carolina changed laws on obscenity and harmful material shown or given to minors. It also lets courts consider sex-offender registration for some of those convictions, starting December 1, 2026. The law also orders a study on a statewide human trafficking reporting system and makes a few technical changes to other laws.

NC-2025-HB832.s: This bill would make a range of changes to North Carolina education rules, including schools, teachers, colleges, and school services.

NC-2025-HB834.s: This law makes changes to how the State Board of Elections works with other agencies on voter registration forms. People who use the online organ donor registry site or apply online for certain licenses or permits may be offered or mailed a voter registration form. It also says the change does not expand online voter registration.

NC-2025-HB920.s: North Carolina enacted a law that sets rules for virtual currency kiosks, which are automated machines used to move money into virtual currency. It requires kiosk operators to give clear warnings about risks, fees, exchange rates, scams, and customer liability before and during transactions, and it lets the state banking commissioner review records and enforce the rules. The law also bans login by QR code or similar scan-based methods and limits access to manual entry methods.

NC-2025-HB925.s: The bill would set a rule for consumer legal funding contracts in civil cases. These contracts would be presumed not to be available in discovery, and consumer legal funding transactions would be presumed not to be allowed as evidence. It would affect people involved in civil lawsuits that use this kind of funding.

NC-2025-HB936.s: The bill would change the rules for robocall and phone ad consent by setting out what counts as prior written permission. It would require a signed written agreement, include the phone number, and clearly tell the person that signing lets the seller send calls and is not required to buy goods or services.

NC-2025-HB958.s: The bill would make changes to North Carolina election rules. It was ratified and later vetoed.

NC-2025-HB96.s: The bill would speed up the removal of unauthorized people from property. It also says that a person who is a tenant is not covered by that part of the rule.

NC-2025-HJR1241.s: This joint resolution honors the life and memory of Louis Milford Pate Jr. and notes his service in the military, as a local leader, and in the North Carolina House and Senate. It also offers sympathy to his family and directs the Secretary of State to send a certified copy of the resolution to them. The resolution took effect when it was ratified.

NC-2025-HJR1243.s: The resolution would adjourn the North Carolina General Assembly on July 2, 2026, and bring it back on July 27, 2026, at noon. It would also limit what lawmakers may take up when they return, including budget bills, constitutional amendments, certain leftover 2025 bills and resolutions, and a few other listed matters. The resolution would take effect when it is ratified.

NC-2025-HJR1244.s: This resolution adjourns the North Carolina General Assembly’s 2025 regular session on July 2, 2026, and sets it to meet again on July 27, 2026, at 12:00 noon. It also limits what lawmakers may take up when they return, including budget bills, constitutional amendments, certain 2025 bills, local bills, appointments, veto overrides, election law bills, and other listed matters. It took effect when it was ratified.

NC-2025-HR1238.s: The North Carolina House resolution honors the Carolina Hurricanes for winning the 2026 Stanley Cup and for their strong 2025-2026 season. It also recognizes the team’s owner, management, and coach, and says the clerk must send certified copies to team members, owner Tom Dundon, and head coach Rod Brind'Amour. The resolution took effect when it was adopted.

NC-2025-HR1239.s: This resolution honors the life and memory of James Michael Clampitt, a former North Carolina House member, and thanks him for his service to his community, state, and country. It also offers sympathy to his family. A copy of the resolution would be sent to his family, and it took effect when adopted.

NC-2025-HR1245.s: This resolution honors the 250th anniversary of the United States and North Carolina’s role in the nation’s founding. It recognizes the state’s history, including the Halifax Resolves and the Mecklenburg Resolves, and honors North Carolinians who served in the Revolutionary War. It also encourages people in North Carolina to take part in events marking the 250th anniversary.

NC-2025-SB1001.s: The bill would change coastal rules and permits in North Carolina. It would raise the maximum fee for processing a CAMA permit application, which is a coastal area permit, and would update some rules for upland basin water standards and financial assurance. It would also make technical fixes to the upland basin permit law and clarify state agency authority over the coastal reserve.

NC-2025-SB1041.s: It would repeal Chapter 126 of the North Carolina General Statutes, the state law chapter tied to public work and personnel rules. It was signed into law on July 6, 2026.

NC-2025-SB1047.s: The bill would rewrite North Carolina rules for guaranteed energy savings contracts used by government units. It would require public notice, a request for qualifications, reviews of bids, and an energy audit before a contract is signed, and it would add rules for how savings are checked each year. It would also make conforming wording changes in other state laws that refer to these contracts.

NC-2025-SB1057.s: The bill would set rules for proxy advisors, which are paid firms that tell shareholders how to vote on company matters. It would require them to say whether their advice against company management is or is not based on a written financial analysis, and to share that analysis on request when they have one. It would also require annual registration with the Secretary of State and a $100 fee. The act would take effect October 1, 2026, and apply to services provided on or after that date.

NC-2025-SB1074.s: The law lets Eden make an agreement with Duke Energy that can block forced annexation of certain Dan River plant land from July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2030, in return for $1,000,000 paid in five yearly $200,000 payments. It also cancels any unified development ordinance the Town of Mills River adopted between June 30, 2025, and July 1, 2026. For Guilford County, it changes the rules for a local 0.25% sales tax referendum and how the tax money would be split and used if voters approve it.

NC-2025-SB1076.s: The law limits how Rocky Mount and Louisburg can move money from their electric utility revenues, and it also limits how Rocky Mount can use natural gas utility revenue. It sets up a Rocky Mount Public Utilities Advisory Committee to review utility rates, budgets, major contracts, service policies, and fund transfers, but the committee can only advise the city. The natural gas and utility revenue limits for Rocky Mount are effective when the law takes effect; the Rocky Mount natural gas part ends on January 1, 2029.

NC-2025-SB1092.s: The act makes a set of Senate and House appointments to many state boards and commissions. It includes appointments to the Southwestern Community College Board of Trustees and the Rockingham Community College Board of Trustees, both for terms ending June 30, 2030. It was ratified into law on August 6, 2026.

NC-2025-SB153.s: This law would let certain state law officers work with federal immigration agents under a formal agreement. It would also bar UNC schools from having rules that limit federal immigration law enforcement and from blocking the sharing of immigration-status information with federal law enforcement, to the extent federal law allows. It applies to UNC constituent institutions and state law enforcement, and it became law after a veto override.

NC-2025-SB177.s: The bill would give the State Board of Elections $15 million in one-time funds for the 2025-26 year to finish upgrades to its election information system and campaign finance software. It would also change state rules so the State Board of Elections can choose to use the Department of Information Technology’s programs, services, or contracts, including tech buying rules, in writing. The same choice would still be available for the General Assembly, the courts, and The University of North Carolina and its schools.

NC-2025-SB227.s: The bill would eliminate “DEI” programs in North Carolina public education. It also adds an exception for single-sex schools, programs, or activities that follow state or federal law.

NC-2025-SB257.s: This act makes base budget appropriations for current operations of State agencies, departments, and institutions in North Carolina for the 2025-2027 fiscal biennium. It sets funding amounts for areas including education, health and human services, agriculture, justice and public safety, general government, and information technology. It also states General Fund availability, reservations of revenue, and unappropriated balances for each fiscal year.

NC-2025-SB355.s: The law makes changes to adult correction work and related court rules in North Carolina. It expands tuition waivers for some survivors and family members of certain public safety workers, updates rules for electronic and satellite-based monitoring, and changes how the Post-Release Supervision and Parole Commission makes some decisions. It also changes how sexually violent predator reviews are done, raises the yearly limit on some purchases from Correction Enterprises to $4,000, and adds more authority for the Department of Adult Correction on substance abuse assessments.

NC-2025-SB445.s: The act changes several state rules on local planning, school testing surveys, and redevelopment. It would change how long some local land-use rights last, limit when local governments can change approved development plans, and set rules for certain uses on redevelopment land. It also lets students take surveys tied to a college admissions test with parent consent and requires notice to parents of 11th graders.

NC-2025-SB474.s: The bill would change the rules on the pause, or moratorium, on county property reappraisals in North Carolina. It also lets a state division consult with the Joint Legislative Commission on Governmental Operations and use people to help with artificial intelligence. It was ratified and signed into law in July 2026.

NC-2025-SB528.s: The bill would direct the Division of Child Development and Early Education to create a workgroup to look at simpler rules for the physical parts of licensed child care centers. The group would include state and local code, fire, health, and child care representatives, and it would study building, fire, and sanitation code issues and report its findings within one year after the act becomes law.

NC-2025-SB558.s: The law sets rules for public colleges and universities in North Carolina, including UNC schools and community colleges, about diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. It bars them from promoting certain race- or sex-based ideas, using some DEI offices or staff, and requiring some courses tied to those ideas, with some speech and research limits left in place. Schools must also certify each year that they are following the law, and the first report had to include early steps and any spending cuts or job changes. The law took effect when it became law.

NC-2025-SB595.s: North Carolina enacted this law to change several tax and revenue rules. It changes parts of the state income tax code, withholding tax timing, and some tax credits, and it also updates rules on timber loss deductions and interest relief tied to past disaster tax bills. The law also shifts vapor directory enforcement to the Alcohol Law Enforcement Division, changes collection rules for tax foreclosure and special assessments, updates credit union and savings bank laws, gives retailers a way to round cash payments because the penny is being ended, and raises pay for members of the Piedmont Authority for Regional Transportation board.

NC-2025-SB602.s: The bill would let owners of certain downtown commercial buildings in Hurricane Helene disaster counties rebuild with the same fire-protection level for windows they had on September 27, 2024, instead of meeting newer state code rules. It applies only to eligible buildings being restored after Helene damage, and owners must file a notarized affidavit with the local building office. The exemption must be claimed within two years after the bill becomes law, and the bill would apply to buildings that get a certificate of occupancy on or after that date.

NC-2025-SB648.s: The bill would change a landlord-tenant law on eviction costs. It would let a landlord recover certain lawyer fees from a tenant in some cases, including when the landlord wins and when a court finds the tenant’s appeal was frivolous, unreasonable, without basis, in bad faith, or just meant to delay the case. The change would apply back to September 9, 2024.

NC-2025-SB675.s: The bill would set rules for charitable groups that are named as beneficiaries of some non-will property transfers, like payable-on-death accounts, insurance, retirement plans, and similar assets. It would let a charity ask for the property or related info with a sworn affidavit and set what papers must be shown, while limiting what personal information the holder of the property can ask for from the charity’s staff or board. It also gives a process and time limits for delivery, court action, and payments back to a donor’s estate if needed. The act would take effect when it becomes law and apply to affidavits delivered on or after that date.

NC-2025-SB801.s: The bill would study ways to protect the personal identifying information of certain Special Operations Forces personnel in North Carolina, and it could lead to a pilot program for eligible active-duty members. It would also let state and local agencies, when feasible, remove or hide that information from public-facing online records after a written request certified by a commander, and the request itself would not be public. Sections 2 and 3 would take effect on January 1, 2027.

NC-2025-SB808.s: The bill would change some dates in the Board of Cosmetic Art Examiners law from October 1, 2026, to December 31, 2026. It would also say that an apprentice license application filed before December 31, 2026, and still pending that day must be granted as a cosmetologist license. Sections 1 and 2 would take effect on December 31, 2026.

NC-2025-SB809.s: North Carolina law removes the 10% cap on satellite annexation for many listed cities and towns, including Spruce Pine. It also removes the Town of Rural Hall from the Forsyth County Countywide Fire Service District. The Rural Hall change takes effect June 30, 2026, and property there will no longer be subject to that fire district tax for tax years starting on or after July 1, 2026.

NC-2025-SB811.s: The act removes the cap on satellite annexations for Bailey, Weaverville, and Cherryville. It also removes listed land from the city limits of Morehead City and Washington, and from Kernersville, Red Oak, Vass, Waynesville, and Walnut Creek. For Walnut Creek, it also limits its city planning powers beyond its contiguous limits and ratifies certain past property actions; most parts take effect June 30, 2026, and the rest take effect when the act becomes law.

NC-2025-SB857.s: The law updates rules for the Funeral Service Board and some licensing rules. It says a funeral establishment that uses a living person's name must have that person licensed as a funeral director or funeral service licensee, or have had a licensed person meet the board's rules when the first permit was issued. It also bars misleading funeral establishment names, including some plural names, deceased names, and names of people not tied to the business.

NC-2025-SB858.s: The law adds one member from the High Point University School of Law to the General Statutes Commission, which helps review state laws. The first appointment from that school runs from September 1, 2026, to August 31, 2029. It became law when signed on June 29, 2026.

NC-2025-SB876.s: The act makes a range of local law changes in North Carolina. It changes how some Rowan County commissioner vacancies are filled, gives Rowan County special rules for taking over planning control from Kannapolis, and moves Kannapolis city elections to even-numbered years with partisan races for mayor and council. It also changes election rules and some vacancy rules for Albemarle and for several Moore County towns, including Aberdeen and Cameron, with some terms extended to match the new election dates.

NC-2025-SB992.s: The bill is about taxation and property taxes.

NC-2025-SJR1088.s: This resolution confirms Floyd McKissick’s appointment to the North Carolina Utilities Commission. He would serve when confirmed until June 30, 2029, filling the rest of Charlotte Mitchell’s term. The resolution became effective when it was ratified on July 2, 2026.

NC-2025-SJR1089.s: The General Assembly confirmed Melanie Bush as director of the Division of Health Benefits in the Department of Health and Human Services. Her term begins when confirmed and runs until June 30, 2029, filling the unexpired term of Jay Ludlam. The resolution took effect when it was ratified.

NC-2025-SJR1090.s: The resolution confirms John Gajda’s appointment to the North Carolina Utilities Commission. He would serve for a term ending June 30, 2027. It took effect when it was ratified.

NC-2025-SJR1091.s: This joint resolution, which was ratified, sets dates for the North Carolina General Assembly to adjourn and return in late 2026. It limits what lawmakers may take up at each return session, such as veto overrides, appointments, election matters, conference reports, and other listed items. It also says the 2025 regular session will end finally on December 18, 2026, and it took effect when ratified.

NC-2025E1-HB3.s: North Carolina law suspends the motor fuel tax from the day after it became law through November 30, 2026, setting the tax rate at zero cents per gallon. It also moves money from a state reserve to help replace funds that would have gone to road, water, wildlife, and cleanup accounts.
